description: We are Miva Ad Astra, developing health monitoring software to help astronauts track and understand their health during space missions. We bring interests and skills in human physiology, data analysis/science , machine learning, and software development. Join us to turn health data into clear, useful insights. We welcome teammates with skills in coding, web development, UI/UX design, data visualization, health sciences and storytelling.
summary:
Team Miva Ad Astra developed **Astrovital**, a web prototype that helps astronauts assess changes in their health when they cannot speak to a flight surgeon in real time. Crew members can log vital signs, sleep, mood, and symptoms. Astrovital compares resting pulse and sleep with the astronaut’s personal baseline, guides a repeat pulse measurement, and gives emergency symptoms immediate priority.

During a simulated communications outage, the app saves a downloadable briefing with the original and repeat readings, measurement conditions, and suggested next steps. Its Mission Replay also lets users compare 85 archived NASA RadLab readings from the International Space Station and attach selected measurements to the briefing as historical environmental context.

Astrovital addresses a practical challenge of long-duration missions. When help from Earth is delayed, crews need to know what to check again, what warrants immediate attention, and what information to preserve for medical review. The prototype demonstrates that workflow using simulated crew health data.
details:
What it does

Astrovital is a web prototype developed by Team Miva Ad Astra to help astronauts assess changes in their health and prepare a briefing when they cannot consult a flight surgeon in real time. Crew members can record blood pressure, resting pulse, blood glucose, temperature, sleep, mood, and symptoms. The app compares resting pulse and sleep with the astronaut’s usual values and explains why a reading was flagged.

How it works and what makes it creative

Astrovital links a flagged reading to a guided recheck. In the fatigue training scenario, an astronaut’s resting pulse rises from a usual 68 bpm to 86 bpm. The app guides the astronaut through a second measurement. A repeat of 85 bpm keeps the review flag visible, and the briefing records both measurements, their timestamps, and the conditions under which the repeat was taken. If the astronaut reports an emergency symptom such as new chest pain, the app immediately displays the onboard emergency instructions.

How we used NASA data

Mission Replay uses 85 archived radiation dose-rate readings from the DosTel1 instrument aboard the International Space Station, available through NASA’s Open Science Data Repository RadLab. Users can compare two readings and attach their values, units, timestamps, and difference to the briefing. The app identifies these as historical measurements of the ISS environment from a different mission. Personal radiation exposure requires personal dosimetry.

Tools and design decisions

We built Astrovital with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript and hosted it on GitHub Pages. It uses an HTML Canvas chart for the NASA data, browser storage for check-ins and briefings, and a service worker designed to make the app available offline after an initial visit. Measurements are entered manually, so the prototype can be demonstrated on a phone or computer without connecting medical hardware. We considered communication delays, ease of use, missing measurements, emergency priority, and clear labeling of simulated crew readings and archived NASA data.

Intended impact

During a communications outage, a crew member can record what changed, repeat a measurement, and save a downloadable briefing for later handoff. That gives the flight surgeon a timestamped account of what the crew observed and checked. We verified the fatigue and emergency scenarios on the live app. The screening rules are for training and require flight medical validation before operational use.
